title: Psalm 47: God Is King of All the Earth
summary: All the peoples are called to clap and shout to God, because the LORD Most High is the great King over all the earth. He has given Israel its inheritance, and he has ascended amid shouts and the sound of the horn. The psalm calls again and again for praise, and it ends with the nobles of the nations gathered as the people of the God of Abraham.
story: Psalm 47 stands between two Songs of Zion, and it widens their view. Psalm 46 saw God protect his city and end war; Psalm 48 will walk around Zion's walls. Between them Psalm 47 lifts the eyes to God's throne and to the whole world he rules. It is one of the enthronement psalms, a group (usually 47, 93, and 95 to 99) that celebrate the LORD as king. Its final verse reaches back to God's promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and forward to the day when the nations join Israel in worship.
historical:
The heading assigns the psalm to the sons of Korah, the Levite singers. Its setting is probably temple worship, but what kind is debated. In the early twentieth century the Norwegian scholar Sigmund Mowinckel proposed that Israel held an annual festival, probably in the autumn, at which the LORD's kingship was ritually celebrated as though he were newly enthroned, and he read Psalm 47 and similar psalms in that light. Many scholars accepted a festival setting of some kind, while others doubted the details, noting that the Old Testament does not describe such a ceremony directly.

Other interpreters connect the psalm with a specific moment: the ark of the covenant being carried up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6, where the ark goes up with shouting and the sound of the horn), or a victory celebration. Still others read it as looking ahead to God's future reign over all nations. These readings can overlap: a psalm used in worship celebrated what God had done, what he was doing, and what he would do.
cultural:
Clapping hands and shouting were the sounds of a coronation in ancient Israel. When Joash was crowned, the people clapped and cried out for the king to live (2 Kings 11:12), and trumpets sounded when Solomon was anointed (1 Kings 1:39). The horn in verse 5 is the shofar, a ram's horn blown to call assemblies, sound alarms in war, and mark sacred occasions. The shout (teruah) could be a battle cry or a cry of acclamation.

The image of God going up (verse 5) most likely pictures him ascending his throne, perhaps symbolized by the ark, which Israel regarded as God's footstool, being carried in procession up to the temple on Zion. Shields in verse 9 stand for rulers, the protectors of their peoples, as the parallel with nobles suggests. The claim that these rulers belong to God is a claim that every earthly authority is under him.
literary: The psalm has two stanzas of roughly equal length. Verses 1 to 4 call for applause and give reasons: God is king, he subdues the nations, he chooses Israel's inheritance. Verses 5 to 9 describe his ascent and call for praise again, with the verb "sing praises" repeated four times in verse 6 alone, and then give reasons: God is King of all the earth, he reigns over the nations, and the nations' nobles gather to him. The two halves follow the typical pattern of a hymn: a call to praise, followed by the reasons for it. The word Maskil appears in verse 7, where it is translated "profound praises", perhaps meaning a skillful or thoughtful song.

outline.t: Clap and shout: the great King chooses his people
God reigns, and the nations gather to him

doctrines.note: The whole psalm is a confession that God is king, not only of Israel but of all the earth. His reign is not a future hope only; he "reigns over the nations" now, even when they do not acknowledge it.

The nations are summoned to worship, and at the end their nobles gather as the people of the God of Abraham. The blessing promised to Abraham for all families of the earth is pictured as reaching its goal.

God chooses Israel's inheritance, the pride of Jacob, whom he loves. His universal reign does not cancel his particular covenant with his people; it is through that covenant that the nations are drawn in.

words.note: Malakh, to reign or be king. "God reigns" (verse 8) is the central confession of the enthronement psalms. Scholars debate whether it should be read as a coronation cry (God has become king) or as a timeless statement (God is king); both fit the psalm's festive tone.

Shophar, the ram's horn. It sounded at coronations, in battle, and on holy days; a day of trumpet blasts opened the festivals of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:24). Its sound in verse 5 marks God's ascent as a royal event.
Abraham. The name is rare in the Psalms, and its appearance here is deliberate. By naming Abraham, the psalm recalls God's promise that through Abraham's family all nations would be blessed.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 47, but the church has long read it on Ascension Day, the feast marking Jesus' ascension into heaven forty days after his resurrection (Acts 1:9-11). The psalm's words "God has ascended amid shouts of joy" first described God going up to his throne on Zion; Christians hear in them the risen Christ going up to reign at the Father's right hand (Ephesians 1:20-22). The gathering of the nations as the people of the God of Abraham is also fulfilled in the gospel. Paul argues that Gentiles who trust Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promise (Galatians 3:7-9, 29). The connection is the church's reading, but it follows the psalm's own direction toward a kingdom that includes all peoples.
questions: The psalm calls all peoples to clap and shout to God. What would it look like for worship to sound like a coronation?
Verse 9 pictures the nations' leaders gathered as the people of the God of Abraham. How does that vision challenge the idea that God belongs to one nation?
How does believing that God reigns now, not just someday, change how you view the rulers and powers of the world?
